Household Economic Positions and the Unequal Security of Family Futures in Chile

Gonzalo Torres RosalesPhD in Sociology, Pontificia Universidad Católica de ChileThe Munich International Stone Center for Inequality ResearchThesis committee: Andrea Canales (ISUC), Rafael Carranza (Gobierno UC), Fabian Pfeffer (LMU) & Patricio Solís (COLMEX)2026

About 20 minutes: thesis map (3 min), Article 1 (12 min), Article 3 (4 min), discussion (1 min).

Insecurity as a social phenomenon: class, planning, and structure

What separates the service class from routine and manual workers is not only how much they earn, but how secure, stable, and promising those earnings are.

Goldthorpe & McKnight 2006; Erikson & Goldthorpe 1992

Class theory treats security as something positions distribute. Research on insecurity measures it household by household, as a risk of loss at one point in time (Western et al. 2012; Hacker et al. 2014).

This thesis treats insecurity as a social phenomenon: it has a relation to class, it is expressed in how households plan their futures, and it takes shape in relations and structures.

Three faces of insecurity

1. Its relation to class

Some facets of insecurity follow class position; others cut across it. Which ones, and what does each reach in children’s lives?

2. Its expression in planning

Secure positions give households control over the future. How does that control become expectations and achievement, and how do peer groups order and align them?

3. Its relational and structural shape

Insecurity arises from combinations of income, occupation, and financial products, within a structure of markets and rights. Which combinations lead to protected positions, and which to vulnerable ones?

Question. How do household economic positions secure family futures, and how much of that security comes from class, from others, and from structure?

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Flipping the baseline (Gambetta 2026): from “who is insecure?” to “how is security produced, and through what?”. Three answers: position (class), others (peer groups that order and align plans), and structure (combinations of resources within markets and rights). Article 1 takes the first, Article 2 the second, Article 3 the third.

Positions, insecurity, and control over the future

Economic position

The household’s market situation in labor, property, and credit (Weber; Waitkus et al. 2024), observed as a configuration of income, assets, debts, and entitlements (Keister et al. 2026).

Class

Employment relations: labor contract or service relationship (Goldthorpe 2010).

Wealth and rights

Secure claims on resources (Dvir-Djerassi & Pfeffer 2025), private or social, on income yet to come (Manduca 2023).

→
Insecurity

The gap between the losses a household may face, often unforeseen, and the claims it can use to absorb them.

It joins the risk of loss from unpredictable events (Western et al. 2012) and the buffers that absorb it (Hacker et al. 2014), with buffers read as claims (Dvir-Djerassi & Pfeffer 2025; Manduca 2023).

Class orders exposure; claims order coverage.

→
Futures

Horizon, investment and achievement, and trajectory.

Security lengthens horizons (Beckert 2024); a favorable position becomes a resource for further gains (DiPrete & Eirich 2006).

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Position is the umbrella concept, built from Weber’s market situation (Waitkus et al.) and observed as a configuration (Keister et al.: multidimensional, nonhierarchical, household-level). Class is the classic reference and the employment component. Wealth follows Dvir-Djerassi & Pfeffer (secure claims) and Manduca (claims on future income; social insurance counts for some uses; claims differ in purpose, transferability, and liquidity). Uses of wealth: purchasing and insurance (Pfeffer & Hällsten 2012), income replacement (Manduca). Beckert: the weight of the security capacity depends on the welfare state. Futures in three planes: horizon (Article 1), investment and achievement (Article 2), trajectory (Article 3).

Wealth functions follow Pfeffer: insurance in Articles 1 and 3 (in Article 1 the coverage comes mostly from contract rights, severance and unemployment insurance, and housing enters only as an exploratory moderator); purchasing and normative in Article 2, where household resources buy a school and with it a set of peers whose norms order expectations and achievement.
Article 1

When Is Economic Insecurity More Than Class?

Contractual Position, Unpredicted Precarity, and Children’s Development and Expectations in Chile

Economic insecurity and unequal futures

The problem: insecurity and class

1

Starting point

Class is a theory of security: employment relations distribute stable contracts and protection (Goldthorpe 2010). Contractual divides also follow position (Emmenegger et al. 2012). Much of insecurity should therefore be class seen from another angle.

2

What position leaves open

Exposure belongs to positions; realization, to events. Two mothers with the same class and the same contract can live very different years: one keeps her job, the other loses it twice.

3

Question

When a mother’s precarity goes beyond what her position anticipated, does it reach her children, and does it reach the same things as class?

4

Constraint on the cause

Whatever explains consequences specific to insecurity must vary within the same position (Gambetta 2026). It cannot be class, education, or a mother’s prior history.

Strategy. Hold position constant by prediction: split lived precarity into the part position anticipated and the part it did not, and compare what each reaches in children’s lives.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Presented as a problem, not a puzzle. Gambetta (2026) is used only for the constraint on the cause: if insecurity has consequences of its own, what explains them must vary within the same position, so position has to be held constant, which is what the decomposition does. The surprising part of the article comes later, in Result 2: losses that position did not anticipate leave capacities intact but lower expectations.

Mothers’ month-by-month work histories, followed into adolescence

Sample

ELPI, a national panel of children born 2006–2009. 6,204 mothers with ≥12 months in the labor force after birth. Attachment is stratified: 44% of working-class mothers meet the threshold vs. 71–75% in other classes.

Precarity, birth to 2012

Mean of three standardized components: share of months unemployed, involuntary exits per active year, share of employed months in precarious contracts (no contract, fixed-term, task, agency, fees).

Class and outcomes

Household EGP class and ISEI before birth (categories in the appendix). Outcomes in 2017 and 2024, after the window: development (assessor, adolescent, caregiver) and expectations (adolescent).

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Months out of the labor force enter neither numerator nor denominator; months in the labor force are controlled in every model. Counting version (Alkire–Foster style): 47% deprived in at least one component, 17% in two or more. Selection: addressed with inverse probability weighting and alternative thresholds (6, 12, 24 months).

Splitting precarity into an expected and an unpredicted part

Lived precarity after the birth is regressed on the mother’s position before it: household class, her education and work history, and residence. The fitted value is expected precarity (36% of the variance); the residual is unpredicted precarity.

Illustration. Two mothers with the same prior position receive the same prediction. If one then loses her job twice and spends months unemployed, that difference is her unpredicted precarity.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Expected precarity is a linear combination of position variables, so its coefficient also absorbs confounding tied to position: read it as a description of what position predicts. The bottom decile of unpredicted precarity is mixed: it includes mothers who moved from precarious to formal jobs and mothers with short spells in the labor force.

What each part should reach, and what was fixed in advance

Resources

Pre-specified

Accumulated deprivation lowers what households invest in children. Expected precarity should lower capacities, as class does.

Disruption

Pre-specified

Unanticipated losses break routines and raise parental stress (family stress model). Unpredicted precarity should reach behavior before cognition.

Horizon

Exploratory

Losses that break expectations of stability lead households to revise plans (Breen & Goldthorpe 1997; Beckert 2016). Unpredicted precarity may lower expectations.

OutcomeClassExpected precarityUnpredicted precarityStatus
Capacities: cognition, mathematics, achievementStrong gradientNegativeNullPre-specified
Behavior problemsGradientWeak or nullHarmPre-specified
Expectations: university, occupational aspirationStrong gradientWeak or nullNegativeExploratory

Fixed in a dated script on October 31, 2026, before the indices were computed: cognition, behavior, and household investments, with a smallest effect of interest of ±0.05 SD. Expectations were added afterward.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Resources: investment and family stress models of economic hardship (Duncan & Brooks-Gunn; Conger & Donnellan). Disruption: family stress model (Conger & Elder); parental job loss and children (Brand 2015). Horizon: relative risk aversion makes educational ambitions depend on perceived risk (Breen & Goldthorpe 1997); security allows long horizons (Beckert 2016; Manduca 2023); parental job loss and middle-class children’s attainment (Kalil & Wightman 2011, to verify). The result: the cognition null was confirmed, behavior passed but is fragile, and the most robust result, expectations, was not pre-specified; it is presented as such.

Result 1: Most lived precarity is position

Class alone explains 8%. Adding the mother’s prior labor history raises it to 31%: precarity is largely inherited from her own past.

60% of post-birth employed months were in a job that started before birth. Top-tercile early precarity: 45% precarious in 2017 vs. 25% in the bottom tercile.

The exception is involuntary exits (5–6%): they behave as events, not as position.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Together with months in the labor force, the final model accounts for 36% of the index. For the precarious-contract and unemployment components, prior history explains 38% and 34%.

Two profiles: durable contracts and job rotation

Monthly labor states after birth, bottom and top third of unpredicted precarity

Expected precarity: top third stays 35 months per job vs. 80 in the bottom third. Job tenure correlates −.51 with it.

Unpredicted precarity: 0.73 jobs per active year; 7% moved to a less protected job after an involuntary exit (<1% elsewhere).

After an involuntary exit, 40% of service-class mothers held a protected job a year later vs. 17% in the working class.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Both top thirds spend about 43% of months in precarious jobs; what differs is movement. Changes of state correlate .36 with expected and .44 with unpredicted precarity. The bottom third of unpredicted precarity combines protected jobs (58% of months) with long spells out of the labor force (31%).

Unpredicted precarity tracks earnings losses and regional job loss

Profile of mothers by decile of unpredicted precarity

Convergent

Higher where regional employment fell (z = −2.99). In the top decile, 60% of mothers earn below 80% of their pre-birth wage.

Discriminant

With resources and traits outside the prediction: |r| ≤ .07, against .16–.29 for expected precarity. Observables explain 3.8% of it.

Stable

Alternative prediction models correlate ≥ .98; a counting version correlates .79 and gives the same results.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
The bottom decile is mixed: mothers who moved from precarious (83% of pre-birth months) to formal jobs, and mothers with short spells in the labor force. Variables in the prediction correlate at zero by construction, and the index components (months unemployed, exits) are part of the index itself: neither counts as validation. Recall error falls mainly on the expected part. Spread differs by class (SD 0.67 service, 0.82 intermediate, 1.26 working); standardizing within class leaves results unchanged.

Result 2: Unpredicted precarity lowers adolescents’ expectations

From p10 to p90 of unpredicted precarity: −3.5 pp expecting university (class: 13.6), −3.9 pp professional aspiration (class: 11.7).

About 0.04 SD per SD. Class gradients are 3–4 times larger, but the profile is different.

Class gradient. Difference between children of service- and working-class households; a contrast between classes, on a wider scale.
Expected precarity. Precarity predicted by the mother’s pre-birth position; mostly durable precarious contracts.
Unpredicted precarity. Precarity that position did not predict; mostly job loss, unemployment, and rotation.

Middle and right panels: per SD of each part, both in the same model, with income-rank splines (2010), months in the labor force, and controls; 40 imputations, longitudinal weights, clustered by comuna. Filled: 95% CI excludes zero.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Expected precarity lowers capacities: cognition −0.070, mathematics −0.049, achievement −0.086. Unpredicted precarity: capacities between −0.011 and 0.007; behavior problems +0.046 (Holm p = .022); self-concept −0.036 (not after correction). Expectations index: −0.048 (expected) and −0.044 (unpredicted). Behavior: p10→p90 implies +0.10 SD vs. a class gradient of 0.29 SD.

Expectations are the most robust result

Smallest effect of interest ±0.05 SD (equivalence logic, Lakens 2017); Holm-corrected one-sided tests.

  • Selection. Reweighting to all mothers with a work history: expectations −0.041, behavior 0.043. Thresholds of 6, 12, 24 months: expectations stay negative (−0.034, −0.041, −0.028).

  • Behavior is fragile. It concentrates among mothers with 12–23 months in the labor force (0.100 vs. 0.021), mostly working class.

  • Confounding. To remove the expectations association, a confounder must explain 4.3% of residual variance; 2010 income explains 0.4%.

  • Timing and bootstrap. Placebo on the 2010 assessment holds; full-procedure bootstrap moves SEs by ≤7%.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Investments: unpredicted precarity lowers household investment about as much as position (−0.046 vs. −0.047) but falls just short of the 0.05 threshold, so by the fixed rule it is inconclusive. Parenting stress in 2012 explains little of the behavior association (0.063 → 0.054).

Slope per SD of unpredicted precarity, main specification with an interaction. Not owned outright: rented, ceded, or paying a mortgage. Only the intermediate-class difference excludes zero (0.144 [0.042, 0.247]).

  • Ownership in Chile concentrates in the working class, largely through subsidized housing.

  • Within the service and intermediate classes, the association with expectations appears among households whose position is not backed by an owned home.

  • Consistent with the insurance function of wealth (Pfeffer & Hällsten 2012). Ownership is uncorrelated with unpredicted precarity (r = −.01).

  • ELPI has no savings or debts, and tenure is measured in 2010, inside the exposure window: a lead, reported as exploratory.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Supplementary Table S8 in Manuscrito_v8. Durable goods show a weaker version of the same pattern (expectations: −0.054 below median vs. −0.026 above). Behavior problems: +0.074 among non-owners vs. +0.022 among owners (difference p = .10).

Contributions, limits, and status

For class analysis

  • Expected precarity, which rests on durable precarious contracts, behaves like class and harms capacities: an extension of class schemas toward their own foundation.

  • Unpredicted precarity is a distinct process, with distinct consequences.

For mechanisms

  • Capacities follow accumulated resources; expectations follow the reliability of the future.

  • Exploratory: harm concentrates where a class position is not backed by wealth.

Limits and status

  • Not causal; residual contains unobservables; mother reports both history and behavior.

  • No data on wealth, debt, or networks: what Articles 2 and 3 take up.

  • Manuscript complete, prepared for journal submission.

Stable contracts would protect children’s capacities; protection against losses would protect their horizons.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
The service-class pattern is consistent with insecurity mattering where losses break expectations of stability (Cooper 2014; Ehrenreich 1989); the working-class behavior pattern with repeated losses at the margin of the labor market wearing on family routines. Both are hypotheses that require data ELPI does not have.
Article 3

A Relational Approach to Economic Insecurity

How Assets and Debts Combine in Chilean Households

Economic insecurity and unequal futures

Household choices happen inside a structure of financial products

We usually explain a household’s security by its decisions: how much it saves, borrows, which products it holds. But those decisions happen within a structure of products that makes some moves close and others distant, and the same debt is not the same insecurity if assets back it.

  • How are households distributed by the relation between their income, debts, and assets?

  • How is the structure of financial products organized, and does it orient movement?

  • From the same position, do households with and without a tertiary credential move differently, and does the structure produce that gap?

Existing measuresWhat they capture
Hacker et al. 2014Large loss not cushioned by liquidity, after it happens
Prieto 2022Count of deprivations: exposure and missing buffers
Prieto 2024Probability of falling into poverty, from household traits
Dvir-Djerassi & Pfeffer 2025Wealth as secure claims; a call for relational financial accounts
This articlePosition before the loss, in balance-sheet magnitudes, located in a structure of products

Relational in three senses: among the household’s own elements, a balance sheet (Result 1); among products, a structure (Result 2); and over time, how position in that structure shapes the way out of insecurity (Result 3).

EFH (Banco Central de Chile): cross-sections 2014–2024 (18,100 households); panel pairs 2014–2024 (4,822); panel 2007–2011–2014 (994). Descriptive design, 30 imputation replicates.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Link to Article 1: this article measures the two elements of insecurity that ELPI could not, magnitude and buffers. Anticipation stays outside. The study is descriptive: it seeks a more complex understanding of household economies given Chile’s financial structure, not causal effects.

Reading the household balance sheet

Each household is placed by three coordinates, all relative to its monthly income. Two of them, liquid buffer and debt burden, define four zones, with cuts at one month and 25%; households are then followed between survey waves and within the structure of products.

Three coordinates

Liquid buffer: accounts, fixed and variable income, in months of income (Hacker’s buffer).

Debt burden: monthly debt payments over income (exposure as a flow).

Net worth excluding housing: in years of income (Prieto’s buffer). It sits beside the zones rather than defining them: 41% hold three years or more, more often poorer and older households, mostly in illiquid goods.

Cuts robust to 15–40% burden and 0.5–3 months of buffer. Arrears are measured in the next wave, apart from the zones. Cross-sections 2014–2024, weighted, 30 imputation replicates.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Zones are a 2x2 of liquid buffer and debt burden. Arrears in the next wave: 7.2% from unbacked debt, 3.2% from the two intermediate zones, 1.5% from protected. Net worth excluding housing is the third coordinate of the state; relative to income it is higher among poorer and older households and is often housing-adjacent or illiquid goods: rich in goods, poor in cash. Source: Art3_conceptualizacion_v3, section 4.

Result 1: Unbacked debt appears at every income level

Same zones, by group

Protection rises with income, from 7% in the lowest quintile to 29% in the highest; unbacked debt stays near one in five in every group.

57% have no buffer and a low burden; the median liquid buffer is zero. Unbacked debt reaches about one in five households in every income quintile.

Zones anticipate problems: arrears in the next wave 7.2% from unbacked debt vs. 1.5% from protected.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Dialogue with Hacker et al. (2014), liquidity as buffer, and Prieto (2022), the Chilean multidimensional index; his non-housing net worth enters as the third coordinate. Cuts robust to 15–40% burden and 0.5–3 months of buffer. Liquidity zero is not homogeneous: among illiquid households, high proximity to liquid instruments raises exit from illiquidity from 10% to 26%.

Result 2: Three circuits of financial products

Three circuits

Consumer credit, financed property, and savings and investment (Louvain, modularity 0.30).

The entry leads to credit

The basic account, held by 83% of households, goes with consumer credit, not with assets. The checking account is the bridge between circuits.

Corrected for frequency

Uncorrected, the network centered on home, vehicle, and accounts because common products are held together. Net of prevalence, income, and life cycle, functional links stand out: mortgage and property, the bank package.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Proximity = partial correlation of co-holding, net of prevalence, income decile, age, education, and household size; negatives set to zero. Strongest links are functional: mortgage with the property it finances, and the bank package. Descriptive, not causal; route and proximity add no predictive power over the state. Next: inverse-probability panel weights, risk grades, relatedness in 2007–2014 pairs. Presented at NUMIC, December 2026.

Result 3: Position in the structure shapes the way out

Households with almost no liquidity

Less than a week of income in liquid assets (61% of panel pairs), by proximity to liquid instruments in the corrected space

ProximityLeave illiquidityAbsorb a shockArrears
Low10%46%3.9%
High26%65%6.3%

Proximity explains leaving illiquidity better than Prieto’s indicators (R² .070 vs. .060). It opens savings and bank credit at once: arrears rise too.

Relatedness

+1 SD of proximity: entry +4.6 pp (base 8.8%), exit −5.8 pp (base 33.4%). None of 100 networks with products reassigned at random produces these effects.

Direction

From a retail store loan, households open a checking account at half the base rate: the credit circuit makes the bank circuit distant.

Division of labor

The balance sheet anticipates realized insecurity (AUC 0.68 vs. 0.60 for Prieto’s index); proximity adds no prediction. Its value is in explaining who moves.

The balance sheet says how exposed a household is; its place among products says which ways out are within reach.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Proximity to liquid instruments: terciles of closeness of the portfolio to checking account, savings account, deposits, and mutual funds in the corrected space. In a model with Prieto’s indicators, high proximity adds 11.7 pp [6.0, 17.4] to leaving illiquidity. In arrears it adds nothing: there, burden dominates. The higher arrears among the proximate is consistent with the checking account bridging savings and bank credit; interpretation tentative. Caveat: proximity is net of income, age, education, and household size, but may still mix with an unobserved general level of financial inclusion. Source: Art3_conceptualizacion_v3, sections 4–7.

Article 3: substantive findings

1. No buffer is the norm

57% of households carry little debt and no backing; the median liquid buffer is zero months of income. Unbacked debt reaches about one in five households in every income quintile.

2. Balance sheets anticipate realized insecurity

Arrears in the next wave: 7.2% from unbacked debt, 1.5% from the protected zone. The three-coordinate state predicts arrears better than Prieto’s index (AUC 0.68 vs. 0.60).

3. Protection is fragile; the unbacked zone persists

38% of protected households fall to no buffer in the next wave; 66% of those without a buffer stay there. Households leave unbacked debt by paying it down, without building liquidity.

4. The product space orients movement

Three circuits: consumer credit, property, savings and investment. Proximity raises entry to an instrument (+4.6 pp) and retention (−5.8 pp in exit). The basic account leads into consumer credit.

5. Liquidity depends on position in the structure

Among illiquid households, those close to liquid instruments leave illiquidity at 26%, against 10% among those far from them.

6. Credential gaps arise outside the structure

From the same zone and income tercile, a tertiary credential adds 5.4 pp in reaching protection, mostly by opening liquid instruments. Observable structure and declared saving explain 20–32% of this gap.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Descriptive, not causal. All measures predict little at household level: realization between waves is largely idiosyncratic. Sources: Art3_conceptualizacion_v3 (18-11-2026), sections 4–7. Persistence and fall figures from the zone transition matrix (panel pairs 2014–2024).

Employment relations

EGP sorts positions by employment status and by how employment is regulated: a service relationship (salary, career, security) or a labor contract (pay for work done) (Erikson & Goldthorpe 1992; Goldthorpe 2010).

Household class

Mother: last job before the birth (work history). Partner: occupation reported in 2010. Coded to EGP and ISEI; the household takes the position of the member with the higher ISEI.

Use in the article

Seven EGP categories and ISEI enter the prediction of expected precarity; the three classes give the class gradient used as a benchmark.

Economic insecurity and unequal futures
Coding with DIGCLASS (Cimentada) from ISCO occupation codes. 69% of households classified at both points are in the same EGP class before the birth and in 2010; both explain precarity almost equally (7.9% and 7.8%). Alternative definitions (mother’s own class, class in 2010, EGP without ISEI, EGP by education) yield predictions that correlate at least .989 with the main one. Known issues: class III is kept whole (Erikson and Goldthorpe suggest grouping IIIb with the working class for women); dominance uses ISEI rather than Erikson’s class ordering; the partner’s class is measured after the birth.
